headline: Prompt caching slashes Claude API bills by 85% for AI agents, setup revealed.
summary: A single configuration change reduced daily costs from $47 to $6.80 for an AI agent processing 4,000 requests, without altering its behavior.
details: An AI agent processing 4,000 requests daily saw its Claude API bill drop from $47 to $6.80 per day. This 85% cost reduction was achieved with a single configuration change, without altering the agent's behavior.

Anthropic's prompt caching works at the prefix level. When a request's prefix matches a previously cached one, those tokens are served from a KV store at a dramatically lower per-token rate. The cache lasts 5 minutes, resetting with each hit, making it ideal for frequently called production agents.

Key candidates for caching include large system prompts (1,000+ tokens), tool definitions (800-1,200 tokens), and few-shot examples (2,000-4,000 tokens). Caching document text for multiple queries against the same document is also highly effective.

The `cache_control` block acts as a "breakpoint" at the end of any message block intended for caching. The API caches everything up to and including this breakpoint, allowing up to four breakpoints per request.

Dynamic content must be placed after the last cache breakpoint to ensure cache hits. If a system prompt is dynamically generated, each variation creates a different token sequence, preventing caching unless static and dynamic parts are separated.

Caching becomes net positive with more than 1.4 requests in a 5-minute window (approximately 17 requests/hour). For agents making around 20 calls/hour with system prompts over 800 tokens, implementing caching is highly recommended.

Developers should always instrument cache usage using the `cache_creation_input_tokens` and `cache_read_input_tokens` fields in the response. This helps verify if the cache is being hit effectively and if the prompt content is truly static.

headline_marked: [[New AI cost-modeling handbook]] uses exact math, finds DeepSeek V3.2 cheapest high-quality LLM
headline: New AI cost-modeling handbook uses exact math, finds DeepSeek V3.2 cheapest high-quality LLM
summary: A new pipeline provides auditable, exact-rational cost modeling for LLMs, moving beyond 'vibes'. It reveals DeepSeek V3.2 as the most cost-effective high-quality open model.
details: Tired of vague LLM cost advice, a new handbook introduces an auditable pipeline for exact-rational cost modeling. This system bypasses floating-point errors and LLM hallucinations in arithmetic, providing precise answers to common agent builder cost questions.

The methodology involves two halves: research agents gather live, cited token prices and benchmarks from the web, storing them in auditable files. An exact-rational computation kernel, `agent-calc`, then performs all calculations, ensuring bit-identical numbers.

The core metric used is 'blended cost ÷ agentic-quality-score', accounting for a production-agentic token mix (85/15 input/output with 75% cache hits). Quality is measured by a normalized agentic score from BFCL, τ²-bench, and SWE-bench Verified.

DeepSeek V3.2 decisively wins as the most cost-effective high-quality open model, due to its low output token price for its tier. DeepSeek V4 Flash on Fireworks is identified as an emerging best deal, offering the cheapest rates with ZDR-by-default and batch discounts.

The handbook also explores complex scenarios, such as optimal traffic splitting across providers, the break-even point for self-hosting, and whether 'smart expensive models' are truly cheaper when accounting for their thinking tokens.

It further investigates the 'cost-of-privacy frontier,' demonstrating how US-jurisdiction privacy requirements impact overall cost. This is solved using linear programming to find optimal resource allocation under various constraints.
